newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Dec inflation to spike, some see 3 pct rise.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Dec inflation to spike, some see 3 pct rise.

text.p: December inflation is expected to spike after a series of wage and price hikes earlier this month, and some economists are anticipating it will exceed three percent -- double November's number.

"The mistake a lot of people have made was to focus on the fact that inflation was slightly better in November. That's irrelevant, it's going to be at least twice the November level," said Gray Newman, economist at HSBC James Capel.
Though not all economists agree, he forecasts at least a 3.2 percent rise in the Consumer Price Index in December, compared with a 1.52 rise in November.

A combination of minimum wage increases, public price hikes, and payment of Christmas bonuses are fueling inflation. Newman also said a slide in the peso in October may also cause inflationary overspill this month.

"While an eight percent hike in gasoline prices (and similar hikes in energy and other prices) had long been expected, increases in transportation tariffs were above expectation," he said in a recent report to clients.

Mexico City's urban buses pushed up fares by 150 percent, while costs of taxis, other collective transport vehicles and subway went up from 27 percent to 33 percent, he said. "Although consumer prices measure national price levels, Mexico City given its size, plays an important role in national price inflation," the report said.

In a recent speech to financial analysts in New York, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz reportedly predicted December inflation would be above three percent, due partly to an increase in the subway fares.
But Alonso Cervera of Interacciones, who predicts a December inflationary blip of up to 2.5 percent, said Ortiz may have been priming the market for a high number in the hope that it comes in lower.
"I think it's an exaggeration to talk of three percent inflation. However, its certainly causing nervousness in the money market," he said.
Most economists agree that even if the size of the December blip catches people by surprise, it will not reflect latent inflationary pressure. "It's purely seasonal," Cervera said.
One factor keeping economists on their toes is the central bank's ability to keep control on growth of the monetary base in December.

According to Christianson, Banco de Mexico has room to let base money expand by 7.5 billion pesos between Dec. 11 and Dec. 31 to remain within its target of 18 billion pesos growth from January to December 1996.

In a recent interview, however, Banco de Mexico Deputy Governor Jesus Marcos Yacaman suggested that the central bank may overshoot the monetary base target, though he said it would be "reasonably close" to the target.
The reason: the December price and wage increases were not expected when the monetary base targets were calculated, and they may affect the demand for money, he said.
